hints: Compare where blood goes next - atria only push blood a very short distance downwards, while ventricles must push blood far out of the heart. What does that difference in distance mean for the work needed?
Think about how wall thickness links to muscle. How does having more cardiac muscle let the ventricles generate the pressure needed to overcome resistance in the arteries?
walkthrough:
Link Wall Thickness to Muscle and Force**
Thicker walls mean more cardiac muscle. More muscle can contract with greater force, so it can generate much higher blood pressure. This is the key structure to function link for the heart.

Why Ventricles Need High Pressure**
Atria only pump blood a short distance down into the ventricles at low pressure. Ventricles must pump blood out of the heart - the right ventricle to the lungs and the left ventricle to the whole body - over a much greater distance and against the high resistance of the arteries. That needs high pressure contraction, so thicker muscular walls are essential.
Final answer: Ventricles have more cardiac muscle to pump blood with more force at higher pressure over a greater distance into the pulmonary and systemic circulations to overcome higher resistance.

hints: For initiating the heartbeat, look for the pacemaker in the wall of the right atrium that sends out regular waves of excitation on its own.
For the delay, think about what sits between the atria and ventricles to hold up the wave so the atria finish contracting first, plus the insulating tissue that stops direct spread.
For spreading through the ventricles, recall the special conducting fibres that run down the septum and then up through the ventricle walls to cause contraction from the base up.
For the valve that closes on left ventricular contraction, remember which valve guards the left side between atrium and ventricle to prevent backflow into the atrium.
walkthrough:
Pacemaker That Starts Excitation**
The sinoatrial node in the wall of the right atrium generates regular waves of depolarisation spontaneously. It sets the rhythm, so it initiates the heartbeat and causes the atria to contract first.

Delay So Atria Empty First**
The atrioventricular node, together with non-conducting tissue between the atria and ventricles, delays the wave for about 0.1 s. This ensures the atria have fully contracted and emptied blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.

Rapid Spread Through Ventricles**
From the AVN the wave passes down the bundle of His and then out through the Purkyne fibres in the ventricle walls. These conducting fibres transmit depolarisation rapidly through the ventricular muscle so both ventricles contract together from the apex upwards, pushing blood into the arteries.

Valve Preventing Backflow on the Left**
When pressure rises as the left ventricle contracts, the left atrioventricular valve, also called the bicuspid or mitral valve, closes. Its cusps snap shut to prevent backflow of blood into the left atrium, so blood is forced into the aorta.

Final answer: initiates heartbeat - sinoatrial node (SAN); delays wave - atrioventricular node (AVN) and non-conducting tissue between atria and ventricles; transmits through ventricles - Purkyne fibres / tissue; closes when left ventricle contracts - left atrioventricular / bicuspid / mitral valve.
